cards.name: Impacted cerumen (earwax)
short: [[cerumen|Earwax]] normally lubricates the canal, traps foreign material and blocks pathogens; it builds up when it is overproduced or pushed in.
Itching, ear fullness and hearing loss with no discharge point to cerumen impaction; infection, discharge, tubes, surgery within 6 weeks or age under 12 mean refer.
Wet wrung-out washcloth over a finger on the outer canal daily prevents impaction; cotton swabs and ear candles are not recommended.
Carbamide peroxide 6.5% in anhydrous glycerin: 5-10 drops, twice daily, up to 4 days; the only nonprescription product she recommends.
No relief after 4 days: contact the primary care provider.

steps.title: Cause and timing: role of earwax and risk factors
steps.q: What does earwax do, and who builds up too much?

rows: The [[eac|external auditory canal]]; wax and water build up there, and the goal is not to damage the [[tm|eardrum]], which conducts sound to the middle ear (T@90689 11/20)
Acts as a {{waterproof barrier}} to pathogen entry
Its {{acidic pH}} and antimicrobial substances inhibit bacterial and fungal growth (handout p. 2; T@91760 11/20)
As cerumen collects debris, the canal moves it outward with jaw movements (handout p. 2)
Some people overproduce earwax, and some push things into the ear, such as cotton swabs (T@91937 11/20)

items: Irritation from foreign objects such as hearing aids or ear plugs
{{Inappropriate removal}} of wax, for example cotton swabs
Atrophy of the ceruminous glands in older adults
Children: the canal is flat and slants downward with growth, so material drains less well in young children (T@92324 11/20)

steps.title: Recognise it: what the patient reports
steps.q: Which symptoms point to impacted cerumen, and which three findings separate it from the other ear disorders?
steps.src: Lam otic slides 8, 23; handout p. 5; T@92615, T@97359 11/20

rows: {{Hearing loss}}, or hearing aid malfunction or feedback
Separates it from a water-clogged ear
{{Itching}} is often present (a water-clogged ear has none)
No discharge; pain is rare and dull if present (swimmer's ear has acute-onset pain and clear discharge)

items: Slide 23 columns for cerumen impaction: pain rare, dull if present; itching often; loss of hearing often; discharge none; sense of fullness or pressure in the ear

steps.title: Self-care or refer?
steps.q: Which findings exclude self-care, and what are the treatment goals?

blocks.text: Exclusions for self-care (slide 10): any one means refer

items: Signs of infection or ear discharge (irritation or rash)
Presence of a ruptured tympanic membrane: abrupt hearing loss and sharp pain
Worsening of the condition after attempted self-treatment

rows: Slide 10: {{<12 years of age}} excluded. Handout p. 3, under carbamide peroxide: {{twelve years and older only}}. Spoken: "children under 12 ... we don't treat children 12 years or under" (T@93413 11/20). A 12-year-old is read differently by the spoken words and the other two
If it looks like an infection, it is an infection, and the pharmacist has nothing to treat it with; the patient sees a doctor (T@92950 11/20)
Slide 8 lists dizziness and vertigo as cerumen symptoms; slide 10 does not list dizziness as an exclusion (slide 26, for water-clogged ears, does)
{{Remove}} cerumen with safe and effective products

steps.title: Treat it: match the product to the situation
steps.q: What does each non-drug measure do, and how is carbamide peroxide used?

rows: Remove cerumen from the {{outermost portion}} of the canal {{daily}}, with the cloth draped over a finger, to prevent impaction

Removes wax manually by insertion into the canal; the handout cautions: risk of trauma to the canal skin or the tympanic membrane. She said the tool is delicate and too deep damages the eardrum (T@94028 11/20)
Warm sterile water with a {{bulb syringe}}; not well studied, and it may not work (handout p. 3; T@94267 11/20)

blocks.label: Impacted cerumen
blocks.title: Carbamide peroxide 6.5% in anhydrous glycerin
pts: FDA-approved nonprescription; the only product she recommends; brand {{Debrox}} (T@94692 11/20)
{{5-10 drops}} into the affected ear(s); remain in the canal for several minutes
Alone or with warm-water irrigation; remaining cerumen is removed with gentle warm-water irrigation with a rubber otic bulb syringe
pick: Carbamide peroxide, per the handout (age rule: see the Self-care or refer step)
Gentle warm-water irrigation with a rubber otic bulb syringe
blocks.move: Move to the primary care provider when symptoms persist after 4 days (slide 16).

blocks.label: Other cerumenolytics
blocks.title: Not recommended: water-based and oil-based agents
pts: Handout p. 4: evidence suggests they are no more effective than water
Water-based examples printed: choline salicylate, docusate sodium, phenazole; oil-based: almond oil, benzocaine
She said they are not recommended anymore and are not as good as carbamide peroxide (T@95576 11/20)

blocks.label: Ear candles
blocks.title: Not recommended
pts: Handout p. 4: potential dangers and injuries, and no scientific evidence
She described hot wax dripping into the ear as not sounding good, and said United States guidelines point to carbamide peroxide (T@95719 11/20)

rows: Soften, liquefy, hydrate or disintegrate cerumen (slide 5)

Water based: acetic acid, Colace, hydrogen peroxide, sodium bicarbonate, sterile saline. Oil based: almond oil, arachis oil, Earex, olive oil, mineral oil. Nonwater, nonoil: Audax (choline salicylate, glycerine) and {{Debrox}} (carbamide peroxide)

A {{1:1 urea-hydrogen peroxide}} complex; it dissociates to release H2O2, which generates effervescing O2, and the effervescence breaks up the wax; catalase in cerumen breaks H2O2 into O2 and water (T@8338 11/18)
An anionic surfactant (-SO3H on the slide) that increases water entry to emulsify cerumen by lowering surface tension between water and cerumen (T@5934 11/18)

steps.title: Counsel and follow up
steps.q: How are ear drops given, and when does the patient return?
steps.src: Lam otic slides 14, 16, 33-34; handout p. 7; T@95193, T@96267, T@99554, T@99717 11/20; her Question 26 answer (emailed 11/20)

blocks.text: Instilling ear drops, adult (slide 33, her Question 26 answer)

rows: Lay a {{folded towel}} on a kitchen or bathroom counter
Lay the head on the towel with the {{affected ear up}}
Gently pull the {{earlobe out and up}} to straighten the auditory tube (her slide's words)
Put the recommended number of drops into the ear canal
Gently {{push on the ear flap}} to encourage the liquid into the ear
Stay lying down for at least {{2 minutes}}

blocks.text: Children and a child who does not stay still

rows: Pull the ear {{back and down}} (slide 33); lie with the affected ear up (handout p. 7)
Hold them down if possible and keep them still for a few minutes, because running around drips the solution out (T@99717 11/20)
A cotton ball over the ear keeps the solution in (T@99554 11/20); the handout: a piece of clean cotton, large enough to remove easily, in the ear for no longer than {{1 hour}} (handout p. 7)

items: Use {{5-10 drops}} twice a day for no more than {{4 days}}
Keep the drops in the canal for several minutes; a cotton ball may be recommended to keep them in place (T@95193 11/20)
Do not use cotton swabs or ear candles; swabs are listed as an inappropriate removal method (handout p. 2)

rows: Contact the primary care provider if symptoms persist after {{four days}} (slide 16)
Pain, burning or irritation of the ear with the medicine
Ear drainage or discharge, dizziness, or recent ear surgery
Slide 34: "indicated after several days of use"

patients.t: A 68-year-old reports fullness in the left ear, itching and slowly reduced hearing for 5 days after trying a cotton swab to clean it. There is no discharge, fever or trauma, and no earlier ear surgery.
patients.q: Which ear disorder is most likely?
o: Water-clogged ear
External otitis (swimmer's ear)
Cerumen impaction
Ruptured tympanic membrane
patients.w: Itching is often present, loss of hearing is often present and there is no discharge: cerumen impaction (slide 23). The cotton swab is a listed risk factor (handout p. 2).

x.Water-clogged ear: A water-clogged ear has no itching (slide 23).
x.External otitis (swimmer's ear): External otitis has acute-onset pain and clear discharge, with a swollen canal and fever (slide 23).
x.Ruptured tympanic membrane: A ruptured membrane gives brief severe pain and abrupt hearing loss, with no itching (slide 24).

patients.t: The patient above is 68, has no signs of infection or trauma, takes no medicine that matters here and has no allergies.
o: Isopropyl alcohol 95% in anhydrous glycerin 5%
Carbamide peroxide 6.5% in anhydrous glycerin
Ear candles
Seek treatment from the primary care provider now
patients.w: A candidate with cerumen impaction: the only nonprescription product she recommends is carbamide peroxide 6.5% (slides 14, 42).

x.Isopropyl alcohol 95% in anhydrous glyce: That is the drying drop for a water-clogged ear (slide 31).
x.Ear candles: Ear candles are not recommended: dangers and no evidence (slide 15; handout p. 4).
x.Seek treatment from the primary care pro: Referral is for patients with an exclusion; this patient has none.

patients.t: A 45-year-old has ear fullness and itching and thinks wax is the cause. They had ear surgery three weeks ago and deny discharge.
o: Carbamide peroxide 6.5% twice daily for up to four days
Warm-water irrigation with a rubber bulb syringe
Refer to a clinician, because ear surgery within 6 weeks excludes self-care
A wet wrung-out washcloth over a finger on the outer canal daily
patients.w: Ear surgery within 6 weeks is an exclusion (slide 10), so the patient is referred even without discharge.

x.Carbamide peroxide 6.5% twice daily for: The drops are for candidates; surgery within 6 weeks excludes self-care.
x.Warm-water irrigation with a rubber bulb: Irrigation is also self-care; the exclusion applies to it too.
x.A wet wrung-out washcloth over a finger: The washcloth is a self-care measure; this patient is excluded from self-care.

patients.t: A mother asks for carbamide peroxide drops for her 9-year-old, who has itching and ear fullness.
o: Give 5-10 drops twice daily for up to four days
Refer the child, because age under 12 is an exclusion to self-care
Use warm-water irrigation at home with a bulb syringe
Recommend a cotton swab to remove the wax
patients.w: Under 12 years of age is an exclusion to self-care for cerumen (slide 10), and she said the ear anatomy in children makes treatment difficult (T@93413 11/20).

x.Give 5-10 drops twice daily for up to fo: That is the adult directions; the age exclusion applies.
x.Use warm-water irrigation at home with a: Irrigation is self-care; the age exclusion applies to the child.
x.Recommend a cotton swab to remove the wa: Swabs are a listed risk factor for impaction, not a treatment (handout p. 2).

patients.t: A 55-year-old used carbamide peroxide 6.5% twice daily for 4 days. The fullness and hearing loss remain.
o: Contact the primary care provider
Continue the drops for 4 more days
Switch to isopropyl alcohol 95% in glycerin 5%
Use an ear candle
patients.w: Symptoms that persist after four days mean contact the primary care provider (slide 16).

x.Continue the drops for 4 more days: The course is up to four days; the plan after that is referral.
x.Switch to isopropyl alcohol 95% in glyce: Isopropyl alcohol dries a water-clogged ear; it is not a cerumenolytic (slide 31).

patients.t: A 70-year-old will start carbamide peroxide drops in the right ear.
o: Lie with the right ear up on a folded towel, pull the earlobe out and up, give the drops, gently push the ear flap, stay down 2 minutes or more
Stand with the head tilted, pull the earlobe down, give the drops, then sit up at once
Lie with the right ear down on a folded towel, pull the earlobe out and up, give the drops, then stay down 1 minute
Sit upright, pull the earlobe back and down, give the drops, and push the ear flap firmly
patients.w: Slide 33: folded towel, affected ear up, earlobe out and up, drops, gentle push on the ear flap, at least 2 minutes lying down.

x.Stand with the head tilted, pull the ear: The ear must be up, and the patient stays down for at least 2 minutes (slide 33).
x.Lie with the right ear down on a folded: The affected ear is up, and the stay is at least 2 minutes (slide 33).
x.Sit upright, pull the earlobe back and d: Back and down is the pull for a child under 3; the adult position is lying down with the ear up (slide 33).

numbers: carbamide peroxide, into the affected ear(s)
symptoms persist: contact the primary care provider
age exclusion on slide 10; handout says 12 and older only
ear surgery within this time excludes self-care
stay lying down after the drops
pull the ear back and down

cards.name: Water-clogged ear
short: Water stays in the [[eac|external auditory canal]] when moisture is retained (hair, narrow canal, wax) or when exposure is high (sweating, humidity, swimming).
No pain, no itching, no discharge; hearing loss and a feeling of fullness or wetness.
Prevent with a towel after bathing, a bathing cap or earplugs when swimming; dry with a hair dryer on the lowest setting.
Isopropyl alcohol 95% in anhydrous glycerin 5%: 4-5 drops, no minimum age (spoken: 70%).
Discharge, pain, dizziness, tympanostomy tubes or ear surgery mean refer.

steps.title: Cause and timing: why water stays in the canal
steps.q: What retains moisture, and who gets it most?
steps.src: Lam otic slide 20; handout p. 4; T@96557, T@96922 11/20

rows: Retention of water within the canal

Hairs in the canal take on volume when exposed to even a small amount of water, which gives the feeling of fullness; it is most common with sweating, humidity and swimming, because the water exposure is constant (T@96557, T@96922 11/20)

steps.title: Recognise it, and tell the ear disorders apart
steps.q: Which findings make a water-clogged ear, and which make an infection?

rows: Pain {{none}}; itching {{no}}; loss of hearing often; discharge none
Cerumen impaction has {{itching}}; a water-clogged ear has none (T@97359 11/20)
[[swimmers-ear|Swimmer's ear]] is an infection with itching and discharge (T@97615 11/20)

blocks.text: Other ear disorders (slides 24-25): she said slide 23 is the main one

rows: Pain brief, severe; no itching; hearing loss abrupt; discharge if associated with ear infection (otitis media)
Pain sharp, steady, unilateral; no itching; hearing loss sometimes decreased; discharge maybe; bulging eardrum, sometimes swollen lymph nodes, dizziness
Dull to severe pain with a sense of fullness; itching yes; hearing loss yes; discharge if associated with infection; if the obstruction is not removed, infection and tinnitus may occur
Pain from sharp to steady to brief and severe; itching rare; hearing loss varies; discharge rarely; untreated hematomas may cause swelling

steps.title: Self-care or refer?
steps.q: Which findings exclude self-care, and what is the goal?
steps.src: Lam otic slides 26-27, 36-37; handout pp. 5-6; T@97876 11/20

blocks.text: Exclusions for self-care (slide 26): any one means refer

items: Signs of infection or ear discharge (irritation or rash)
Presence of a ruptured tympanic membrane: abrupt hearing loss and sharp pain
Worsening of the condition after attempted self-treatment

rows: Use a safe and effective agent
A 12-year-old with wetness, fullness and ear discharge after swimming lessons, with tympanostomy tubes placed at age 4: {{not a candidate}}; the mother contacts the pediatrician immediately
Slide 26 excludes under 12; slide 31 says isopropyl alcohol has no minimum age; slide 29 puts water-absorbing earplugs at children over 11. The slides print all three

steps.title: Treat it: prevent, dry, then use the drops
steps.q: What prevents water from staying in the ear, and what dries water already there?

blocks.text: Prevent water from entering or staying (slide 29; handout p. 6)

rows: Wipe the ears well with a {{towel}} after bathing or showering
A {{bathing cap}} or earplugs when swimming protect the ears from water (spoken: earplugs and bathing cap keep water out, T@98127 11/20)
Cotton balls coated with petroleum jelly
Handout: for water exposure of less than 15 minutes; she said she knows no one who likes the feeling, but the guidelines allow it (T@98398 11/20)
Handout: for water exposure of more than 15 minutes

blocks.text: Dry water already in the canal (slide 30; handout p. 6)

rows: {{Children over 11}} (slide 29); insert into the canal and leave in {{5-10 minutes}} to absorb trapped water, then remove and discard; they absorb only a little water and do not prevent water from entering during bathing or swimming (handout; T@98558 11/20)
Pull the lobe gently and tilt the head downward so the water drips out (handout; T@98781 11/20)
Blow dryer on the {{lowest heat}} setting to help dry the canal; not the highest setting (handout; T@98858 11/20)

Instill {{4-5 drops}} in the affected ear

patients.t: A mother brings her 14-year-old son. Since a swim meet he has wetness, fullness and ear discharge. He had tympanostomy tubes placed at age 3.
patients.q: What is the most appropriate intervention?
o: Isopropyl alcohol 95% in anhydrous glycerin 5%, 4-5 drops
A water-absorbing single-use earplug for 5-10 minutes
Carbamide peroxide 6.5% twice daily
The mother should contact the pediatrician immediately
patients.w: Tympanostomy tubes and ear discharge are exclusions to self-care (slides 26, 36-37), so the answer is referral.

x.Isopropyl alcohol 95% in anhydrous glyce: The drying drops are for candidates; tubes and discharge exclude him.
x.Carbamide peroxide 6.5% twice daily: Carbamide peroxide is for cerumen and is self-care too.

patients.t: A 25-year-old swimmer has fullness, wetness and muffled hearing after training. There is no pain, itching or discharge, and no ear tubes or surgery.
o: Carbamide peroxide 6.5% in anhydrous glycerin
Isopropyl alcohol 95% in anhydrous glycerin 5%
An ear candle
A cotton swab dipped in water
patients.w: No pain, no itching, hearing loss and fullness or wetness: a water-clogged ear; the drying drop is isopropyl alcohol (slides 23, 31).

x.Carbamide peroxide 6.5% in anhydrous gly: That product removes cerumen; this patient has no itching or wax findings.
x.A cotton swab dipped in water: A swab is not a listed treatment; swabs are a risk factor for impaction (handout p. 2).

patients.t: A 30-year-old has acute ear pain, itching, clear discharge, a swollen ear canal and a fever.
patients.q: Which disorder is this, and what is the plan?
o: Water-clogged ear; use isopropyl alcohol drops
Cerumen impaction; use carbamide peroxide
Swimmer's ear (external otitis), an infection: refer
Foreign object; use irrigation
patients.w: Acute onset pain, itching and clear discharge with a swollen canal and fever are external otitis (slide 23). It is an infection, so refer (T@92950 11/20).

x.Water-clogged ear; use isopropyl alcohol: A water-clogged ear has no pain, itching or discharge.
x.Foreign object; use irrigation: Foreign objects are not described with clear discharge and fever; infection is not self-treated.

patients.t: A 40-year-old used isopropyl alcohol 95% in glycerin 5% for 10 days. The fullness and hearing loss remain.
o: Use the drops for 10 more days
Switch to carbamide peroxide 6.5%
Use a hair dryer on the highest heat
See the primary care provider
patients.w: No benefit after several days of use (spoken: 7 days) means refer (slide 34; T@100235 11/20).

x.Use the drops for 10 more days: Ten days already exceeds both the printed and the spoken limits.
x.Switch to carbamide peroxide 6.5%: Carbamide peroxide treats cerumen; the plan after no benefit is referral.
x.Use a hair dryer on the highest heat: The dryer is used on the lowest heat setting (handout).

patients.t: A recreational swimmer gets water in the ears every summer and asks how to prevent it.
o: Put carbamide peroxide drops in both ears before each swim session
Towel the ears dry after bathing, and wear a bathing cap or earplugs to swim
Burn an ear candle in each ear after every swim to draw the water out
Clean both ear canals with a cotton swab after every swim to remove water
patients.w: Prevention (slide 29): towel after bathing or showering, bathing cap or earplugs when swimming.

x.Put carbamide peroxide drops in both ear: Carbamide peroxide is a cerumenolytic, not a preventive.
x.Burn an ear candle in each ear after eve: Ear candles are not recommended (slide 15) and are not a listed measure here.
x.Clean both ear canals with a cotton swab: Swabs are not a listed measure; they are a risk factor for impaction (handout p. 2).

patients.t: A patient asks how to use a hair dryer to dry the ear canal.
o: Use the highest setting for a short time
Use the lowest heat setting
Hold it against the ear canal
Use it only after isopropyl alcohol drops
patients.w: The dryer is used on the lowest heat setting (handout p. 6; T@98858 11/20).

x.Use the highest setting for a short time: Do not use the highest setting (T@98858 11/20).
x.Hold it against the ear canal: Holding it against the canal is not in her instructions.
x.Use it only after isopropyl alcohol drop: The dryer and the drops are separate options.

la.text: FDA-approved nonprescription product for hardened or impacted cerumen. 5-10 drops into the affected ear(s), remaining in the canal for several minutes; twice daily for up to four days. Contact the primary care provider if symptoms persist after four days.

docusate-otic.name: Docusate sodium (Colace), water-based cerumenolytic

sk.text: A water-based cerumenolytic (slide 6). An anionic surfactant (-SO3H on the slide) that increases water entry to emulsify cerumen: it lowers surface tension between water and cerumen by dissolving in both media through lipophilic and hydrophilic functional groups (slide 7). It is a stool softener on the slide. It is a topical agent; an ionic molecule is not expected to be absorbed well, so systemic effects are not a worry (T@7059 11/18).
sk.src: Sikazwe OOO slides 6-7; T@4901, T@5934, T@7059 11/18

how.text: An anionic surfactant that increases water entry to emulsify cerumen by lowering surface tension between water and cerumen; it dissolves in both media through lipophilic and hydrophilic functional groups.

la.text: Not recommended. Her handout lists docusate sodium among the water-based agents (with choline salicylate and phenazole) whose evidence suggests they are no more effective than water; she said the water-based and oil-based agents are not recommended anymore and carbamide peroxide is the only product to recommend.

counsel: Dr. Lam does not recommend water-based or oil-based cerumenolytics; the nonprescription product she recommends is carbamide peroxide 6.5% in anhydrous glycerin.

eac: The canal that leads from the outer ear to the tympanic membrane; wax and water build up there.

swimmers-ear: An ear infection with acute-onset pain (mild to severe), itching, clear discharge and a swollen ear canal; it is not treated with the self-care products.

tell.title: Water-clogged ear, cerumen impaction or swimmer's ear

a: No → **water-clogged ear** (no pain, no itching, no discharge)

path.q: Is there discharge or acute-onset pain?
a: Yes, clear discharge and acute pain → **swimmer's ear**, an infection: refer
No discharge, pain rare and dull → **cerumen impaction**

rows: Itching separates the water-clogged ear from the other two.
Discharge makes it an infection: refer.
Sense of fullness or pressure in the ear
Swollen ear canal, stuffiness, fever, swollen lymph nodes

No → pull the earlobe **out and up**

pairs.title: Carbamide peroxide or isopropyl alcohol ear drops?
a: impacted cerumen; 5-10 drops, twice daily, up to 4 days; follow up after 4 days
b: water-clogged ear; 4-5 drops; no minimum age; follow up after several days (spoken: 7)
pairs.same: Both are nonprescription otic drops in anhydrous glycerin, given into the affected ear with the same lying-down steps.
profs: Carbamide peroxide is the only nonprescription cerumenolytic she recommends (T@94692 11/20); isopropyl alcohol is a drying agent (slide 31).
Carbamide peroxide releases H2O2; catalase turns it into O2, and the effervescence breaks up the wax (slide 8).

pairs.title: Debrox or Colace?
a: nonwater, nonoil based (Sikazwe slide 6); releases H2O2 then O2; the product she recommends
b: water based (Sikazwe slide 6); anionic surfactant that lets water into the wax; she does not recommend water-based agents
pairs.same: Both are cerumenolytics: they soften, liquefy, hydrate or disintegrate cerumen.
profs: Slides 5-8; Colace is a surfactant, Debrox an oxidizer that makes oxygen bubbles.
Handout p. 4 and slide 15: other cerumenolytics are not recommended; carbamide peroxide is the one to recommend.
